questions.q: What was the Meridian-CICD-Operator role actually meant to be scoped to, versus where it was assigned?
options: Meant for the whole subscription, but assigned only to a single VM
Meant for rg-meridian-shared-net, but never actually assigned anywhere
Meant for a different Azure tenant entirely
Meant for rg-meridian-prod-app only, but assigned at the whole subscription scope
questions.explain: The role was intended for routine deployment operations in one resource group, but the assignment itself was made at the subscription level under deadline pressure.

questions.q: Why did Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachineScaleSets/* make the role more dangerous than intended?
options: It granted every action on every VM scale set under that provider, not just restart-and-scale, reaching scale sets outside the deployment pipeline's actual job
It only applied to storage accounts, not compute resources
Wildcard actions are automatically rejected by Azure RBAC and have no effect
It granted access to AWS resources through a cross-cloud trust relationship
questions.explain: A resource-provider wildcard grants every action under that provider, which is far broader than the restart and scale actions the pipeline actually needed.

questions.q: How did this misconfiguration actually get discovered?
options: Through a scheduled, formal access review that specifically checked custom role assignments
The CI/CD service principal's credentials were compromised, which revealed the over-broad access
A Defender for Cloud identity-and-access posture recommendation flagged unusually broad service principal access, which a security engineer then traced with az role assignment list
Meridian's finance team noticed an unexpected billing increase
questions.explain: It surfaced sideways, through a routine Defender for Cloud posture recommendation, not through a dedicated audit or an actual incident.

questions.q: Why does the case study call this misconfiguration dangerous even though the service principal never actually used most of what it could reach?
options: Because unused permissions are automatically revoked by Azure after 90 days regardless of configuration

Because the blast radius of a future credential compromise was set by this assignment long before any incident occurred -- a compromise would have reached the whole subscription, not just one resource group
Because Defender for Cloud charges extra for unused role assignments
Because unused permissions always trigger an automatic security incident
questions.explain: The real risk wasn't current misuse -- it was that a future compromise of this identity would inherit subscription-wide reach instead of being contained to one resource group.

questions.q: What was the preferred long-term fix over continuing to hand-patch the custom role?
options: Deleting the CI/CD service principal entirely and running deployments manually
Re-scoping the assignment to the subscription's root management group instead of a resource group
Combining Azure's built-in Virtual Machine Contributor and Monitoring Reader roles, scoped to the one resource group, instead of maintaining a custom role at all
Granting the role Owner permissions to simplify future troubleshooting
questions.explain: Built-in roles, correctly scoped, covered the same operational need without a custom role definition to maintain -- removing the exact category of mistake that caused this incident.
